notes: Personal injury appeal on spontaneous suspension failure; liability and causation findings upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Clough v P&O: appeal on lorry suspension unit failure causation
key_facts: Mr Clough, a mechanic, injured his hand when an offside air-suspension piston on a P&O trailer allegedly broke apart at the defendants' premises in December 1999.
The county court judge found external force applied by the claimant was the more likely cause rather than spontaneous failure of a cracked unit under limited pressure.
The claimant also argued missed October inspections caused the crack; the judge held it was speculative when the crack appeared.
Expert evidence shifted after a late witness statement about re-pressurisation timing, but the judge preferred the defendants' engineer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from St Helens County Court dismissal of a personal injury claim against P&O Trans European (Holdings) Ltd.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the trial judge was entitled to find the accident was not caused as the claimant contended and that missed inspections did not cause the failure on balance of probabilities.
enrichment.ratio: An appellate court will not overturn a trial judge's choice between two equally possible expert explanations where the judge properly directed himself on the balance of probabilities, had regard to credibility and background, and made explicit causation findings on inspection evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the judge misunderstood agreed expert evidence on spontaneous failure under limited pressure
Whether paragraph 20 of the judgment was inconsistent with the joint experts' views
Whether failure to inspect in October probably caused the cracked piston to remain undetected
Whether the judge erred in preferring external force over spontaneous failure

confidence.notes: Liability, causation and appellate reasoning are clearly recorded.

notes: Vexatious litigant strike-out; extensive procedural history and clear disposal on HRA and judicial act points.

enrichment.short_title: Branch v DCA: strike out of Human Rights Act claim against courts
key_facts: Anthony Branch and family members sued the Department for Constitutional Affairs and several courts alleging Convention breaches, anti-Semitism and collusion with third parties.
Master Turner had struck out courts as defendants; the Attorney General later obtained a section 42 order against Mr and Mrs Branch.
The particulars relied on numerous prior judgments and orders, including companies petitions and county court decisions, as wrongful DCA conduct.
The defendant applied to strike out the claim as disclosing no reasonable grounds and an abuse of process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under CPR 3.4(2)(a) to strike out particulars of claim, adjourned with a civil restraint order application.
enrichment.outcome: Particulars of claim struck out in their entirety; no reasonable grounds disclosed and complaints about judicial acts could only be pursued by appeal or judicial review routes.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings under section 6 of the Human Rights Act against the DCA cannot be used to collaterally attack judicial decisions; complaints about judicial acts must be brought by appeal or judicial review, and the Crown has absolute immunity under section 2(5) of the Crown Proceedings Act 1947 for judicial acts.
legal_issues: Whether the claim disclosed reasonable grounds under CPR 3.4(2)(a)
Whether section 9 of the Human Rights Act barred the claim in respect of judicial acts
Whether section 2(5) of the Crown Proceedings Act 1947 provided an absolute defence
Whether the action was vexatious or an abuse of process

notes: Major CGT residence appeal; Park J's detailed corporate residence analysis and allowance of appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Wood v Inspector of Taxes: corporate residence in CGT avoidance scheme
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Ron Wood implemented a scheme to shelter capital gains on sale of Ron Wood Greetings Cards group shares via Holdings and offshore vehicles.
Copsewood Investments Ltd, managed from Geneva, sold Holdings to Eulalia Holding BV, a Netherlands company, to avoid CGT on the 49% stake.
The Revenue assessed that Eulalia was UK-resident despite Netherlands incorporation, defeating the scheme's central assumption.
Special Commissioners upheld the assessment on common law central management and control and statutory effective management tests.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Chancery Division from the Special Commissioners on corporate residence for capital gains tax purposes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Park J held Eulalia was not shown to be non-resident and the Special Commissioners erred in finding UK residence.
enrichment.ratio: Corporate residence turns on where central management and control actually abides; merely signing resolutions in a jurisdiction without informed effective decisions there does not establish residence, and the place of effective management is where effective management decisions are taken.
legal_issues: Whether Eulalia was UK-resident under common law central management and control principles
Whether Eulalia was UK-resident under section 249 of the Finance Act 1994
Whether Barclaytrust-managed BVI and Netherlands companies exercised real management in the Netherlands
Whether the CGT scheme failed if Eulalia was UK-resident
linked_authorities: De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd v Howe [1906] AC 455
Unit Construction Co Ltd v Bullock [1960] AC 351

notes: Leading costs appeal on proportionate awards, mediation and Part 20 proceedings in building dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Burchell v Bullard: costs after builder's claim and exaggerated counterclaim
key_facts: Builder Mr Burchell claimed about £18,000 for extension works; homeowners counterclaimed over £100,000 including alleged roof rebuild costs.
The recorder gave separate judgments, ordering defendants to pay the net £5,026 difference but each party to pay the other's costs on claim and counterclaim.
Defendants recovered only about 15% of their counterclaim and had refused early mediation offered before litigation.
Total costs exceeded £185,000 on a £5,000 judgment; the builder also faced Part 20 subcontractor costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against costs orders following a five-day Bournemouth County Court trial with Part 20 proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defendants ordered to pay 60% of the claimant's costs of the claim, counterclaim and Part 20 proceedings and 60% of his liability to the Part 20 defendant, plus appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party wins overall in claim-and-counterclaim litigation, CPR 44.3(6)(a) permits a proportionate costs order rather than rigid costs-follow-the-event on each claim; unreasonable refusal of mediation may inform conduct, and joining a subcontractor in a roof dispute was a reasonable Part 20 step.
legal_issues: Whether the recorder erred by ordering separate costs on claim and counterclaim without a proportionate order
Whether the Part 20 claim against the roofer was unreasonable
Whether defendants' refusal of mediation warranted a costs sanction
How to identify the unsuccessful party where net judgment favoured the builder

enrichment.short_title: Smurthwaite v Simpson-Smith: permission on costs after withheld disclosure
key_facts: Mr Smurthwaite sought to set aside a voluntary arrangement supervised by insolvency practitioner Mr Mond after a defective Ferrari purchase from Mr Simpson-Smith.
A deputy judge dismissed an application for specific disclosure and summarily assessed £6,000 costs against Mr Smurthwaite.
Over 100 documents were disclosed shortly after the hearing, contrary to representations that no further documents existed.
Laddie J dismissed a review application and awarded further costs of £10,600.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal interim disclosure and review orders ahead of a fixed Chancery trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on the costs order only with a stay of execution; remaining grounds adjourned until after trial and the Laddie J application adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: Where respondents misled the court about possession of documents at a disclosure hearing, there is a real prospect that a costs order against the applicant should be set aside; other grounds may be premature before trial and misrepresentation is best addressed at first instance.

Whether costs should be repaid because documents were withheld at the hearing
Whether Diane Williams was an associate or reputed wife under section 435(8)

notes: Important post-tariff lifer Parole Board JR; Walker J declaration on section 32(6) and detailed Article 5.4 analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Girling v Parole Board: post-tariff release, directions and Article 5.4
key_facts: Mr Girling, a post-tariff mandatory lifer convicted of murder in 1984, was refused release by the Parole Board in October 2004 despite acute leukaemia.
The Board cited unchanged risk factors, lack of programme engagement and absence of a suitable release plan.
He challenged medical evidence handling, linking risk to release plans, and Parole Board independence given Home Secretary directions and referral gateway.
Home Secretary directions of August 2004 required consideration of resettlement plans before directing release.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review of a Parole Board refusal to direct release and challenges to statutory scheme and directions under Article 5.4.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; declaration made that section 32(6) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 does not apply to the Parole Board's judicial functions; no order for reconsideration or costs against defendants.
enrichment.ratio: Section 32(6) of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 cannot authorise the Home Secretary to direct the Parole Board on matters to be taken into account when exercising judicial release functions under section 28; however an erroneous belief that such directions applied does not vitiate a decision where their content was innocuous and causatively irrelevant.
legal_issues: Whether the Parole Board failed to consider medical evidence on risk
Whether linking risk to absence of a release plan was lawful
Whether Home Secretary directions compromised Parole Board independence under Article 5.4
Whether section 28 gateway and timing provisions breached Article 5.4

notes: High-profile libel trial on Hamilton investigation; lengthy justification analysis with clear dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Miller v Associated Newspapers: justification of Hamilton inquiry criticism
key_facts: Detective Chief Superintendent Christopher Miller sued Associated Newspapers over Daily Mail and Evening Standard articles criticising the Neil Hamilton sex-assault investigation.
Articles said the Yard admitted the Hamiltons should never have been arrested and the inquiry would cost about £1m.
The investigation followed false allegations by Nadine Milroy-Sloan; Miller was crime manager at Redbridge with wide responsibilities.
Associated Newspapers pleaded justification via Lucas-Box meanings alleging management failures and poor decision-making.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Queen's Bench Division of a libel claim with a substantive defence of justification.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the defendant proved the defamatory allegations substantially true and there was judgment for the defendant.
enrichment.ratio: A defendant need not prove a claimant was solely responsible for investigative failures to succeed in justification where Lucas-Box meanings allege shared responsibility for delays, management failures and wrongful arrest; partial leaked information may still support substantial truth if core allegations are proved.
legal_issues: Whether the articles bore defamatory meanings critical of Mr Miller's conduct
Whether Associated Newspapers could justify allegations of investigative shambles
Whether Mr Miller was solely or partly responsible for the Hamiltons' arrest
Whether reasonable grounds existed for publication at the time

notes: Vexatious litigant Ewing planning challenge; delay fatal to 2003 permissions with call-in procedural comment.

enrichment.short_title: Ewing v ODPM: vexatious litigant planning challenge at Weston-super-Mare
key_facts: Mr Ewing, subject to a section 42 vexatious litigant order, sought to challenge North Somerset planning permissions for Royal British Legion redevelopment at Beach Road, Weston-super-Mare.
Permissions granted in January and December 2003 involved demolition of Severn Croft in a conservation area; a November 2004 resolution was not yet formally issued.
English Heritage objected that Severn Croft made a positive contribution; the council concluded overall redevelopment would preserve and enhance the conservation area.
The ODPM refused revocation, finding the decisions were not grossly wrong in the national interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined section 42(3) permission application and permission to apply for judicial review heard orally by Ouseley J.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on all grounds; 2003 challenges failed for delay, November 2004 challenge unarguable on PPG 15, and call-in/refusal points not warranting relief though a fresh call-in application could be made.
enrichment.ratio: Challenges to conservation-area demolition permissions must consider the application as a whole under PPG 15; it is not unlawful to permit demolition of a positively contributing building where overall redevelopment preserves or enhances the area, and revocation/refusal policies lawfully set a high national-interest threshold.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Ewing should be granted section 42 permission to proceed
Whether delay barred challenges to 2003 planning permissions
Whether the council misapplied PPG 15 on demolition of Severn Croft
Whether the Secretary of State unlawfully fettered discretion on revocation or call-in

confidence.notes: Permission refusal and planning law reasoning are clear; call-in point addressed procedurally only.

notes: Case stated on PACE Code D parade requirement; Forbes applied with section 78 fairness upheld.

enrichment.short_title: McKenna v DPP: identification parade and recognition evidence fairness
key_facts: Jason McKenna was convicted of driving while disqualified and without insurance after Special Constable Newlyn recognised him driving a Mazda at Allround Cars in Strood.
The officer had known McKenna about 14 years earlier through solicitors' work and had seen him only once since about 1990.
No identification parade was held despite McKenna disputing he was the driver.
McKenna admitted owning the car previously and using the garage where the incident occurred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Maidstone Crown Court on PACE Code D and section 78 admissibility issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; failure to hold an identification parade breached Code D but admitting the recognition evidence was fair under section 78.
enrichment.ratio: PACE Code D imposes a mandatory parade obligation unless the suspect is well known to the witness or a parade would serve no useful purpose; prior acquaintance years earlier without recent contact does not make the suspect well known, yet strong recognition evidence coupled with admissions may still be fairly admitted under section 78.
legal_issues: Whether failure to hold an identification parade breached Code D paragraph D:3.12
Whether the witness's prior acquaintance made a parade futile as a recognition case
Whether the identification evidence should have been excluded under section 78
Whether the Crown Court erred in upholding conviction
linked_authorities: R v Forbes [2001] 1 Cr App R 430

notes: Attorney General contempt application for publishing private Children Act judgment; undertakings accepted in lieu of imprisonment.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney General v Pelling: contempt for publishing private family judgment
key_facts: Michael Pelling published a private Children Act judgment by HHJ Goldstein in his journal Contact and on the internet.
The Attorney General applied for committal for criminal contempt of court after prolonged procedural challenges and adjournments.
Pelling had previously been involved in family proceedings concerning his son Alexander and acted as a McKenzie friend.
The court found contempt proved but accepted undertakings under section 12 in lieu of imprisonment, with costs against the defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's application for committal or other penalty for publication of information relating to private family proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Defendant found guilty of contempt; undertakings under section 12(1)(a)(ii) of the Administration of Justice Act 1960 accepted in lieu of imprisonment and a costs order made.
enrichment.ratio: Publication of a private Children Act judgment knowing the proceedings were private constitutes criminal contempt; where undertakings adequately protect confidentiality and the publisher cooperates, the court may accept them in lieu of immediate imprisonment despite the gravity of the breach.
legal_issues: Whether publication of the private judgment constituted criminal contempt
Whether procedural defects in the Attorney General's application should strike out the committal
What sentence or penalty was appropriate for the contempt
Whether Article 10 free expression justified publication
